utterances.text: Could that be done within the next 15 or 30 seconds, Mr. Hedaraly. Let's proceed for the time being and the invitation to deal with the collection/reception centres seems to be relevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, on the topic of reception centres, you stated that you were only assigned to collect those people remaining, that were not capable of living on their own and there was no plan or directive to collect people who were capable of living by themselves. And you also stated that the authorities would not transfer people to the reception centres against their will. My question is, would you be able to explain why there's information that civilian women, children, and men were brought to reception centres against their will and that they were guarded --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we have some references, Mr. President, please. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I'm not sure whether or not it's actually in dispute that there's evidence in this case so far on what I'm putting to him, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is very much in disputes, Mr. President, and if I can just state now my general objection to this. The procedure thus far has been to put factual questions to a witness and then confront him at the end with the argument if that is what is. I don't deny that it's possible to do it in reverse, but then I think the person is required, if you start from the back, that you're going to lay the foundation then for the ultimate question subsequent to that. We've been proceeding now with counsel giving essentially his views of the evidence which is disputed. So if we can go step by step and see exactly what it is that's the basis for the question, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, of course, we might have another problem, that what is -- Mr. Carrier is blamed for putting the evidence to the witness, but now he does it in a rather general way. Let's say that we have various types of evidence, disputed or not, but which relates to this matter. Let me just consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, let me put one or perhaps two questions to the witness first. Mr. Zidovec, do you know of any case where civilians were taken to a centre - and I'm talking about civilians at this moment - where they were taken against their will? And for this moment, I'm not making any distinction between whether it is a reception centre or a collection centre. Are you aware of any case where this may have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the reception centre closest to the city of Knin was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is not a precise answer, an approximate answer. Could you tell us approximately would have been the distance between the town of Knin and the reception centre you remember as being closest to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note that there were centres in Knin, Obrovac, Benkovac, and Zadar. I know of a centre located on an island opposite Sibenik, the island of Obonjan, which was the longest lived. But I suppose that the centre could have been housed in a school building or in the vicinity of the Knin hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a reception centre established in Knin town itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember where that was located, in what kind of building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't know. I can only guess that it may have been in a school building or the gym of a school. I can't give you an exact answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you exclude for the possibility that someone was taken to a school building in Knin, being a civilian, and would have to stay there for a while, although that person did not wish to go there and to stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall ever seeing an account of a civilian having been forcibly taken to a reception centre for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us as far as collection centres and reception centres are concerned, was there, to your knowledge, a reception centre in Knin town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a moment ago that I believed that there existed for a while a reception centre for civilians in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about a collection centre, and apparently a distinction is made between a sabirni centre and I think what is called a prihvatni centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a problem in interpretation. To the best of my recollection, there was a reception centre for civilians, which operated for a while in Knin. If my memory is correct, eventually, to improve the general conditions, it was transferred to Zadar, I believe, although I don't know how many civilians were willing to go there at all. There is one information I know of certainly, and that's according to the information of the civilian protection, a bit under a thousand individuals, 960 or 980 of them, passed through the reception centre in Knin. The information can be found in the final report of the civilian protection in the implementation of Operation Povratak, following Storm. The report was compiled in early December of 1995. Based on the information I know of, which comes -- comes from the report, I can tell you that when it comes to reception centres for civilians across the territory covered by Operation Storm, and I'm pointing out that I'm referring to the entire territory, a bit under 4.000 persons went through these centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about those centres. Do you know when the reception centre in Knin was established? I'm talking about the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it right at the beginning of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may have happened in the first half of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as a collection centre, sabirni centre is concerned, was there one established in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if such a centre was set up in Knin, because it was not the focus of our interest. The document shown to me by the Prosecution here clearly indicates that the criminal investigation police engaged in preparations for the setting up of collection centres. This is something I saw in the document from the specialist meeting of the chief of the crime police sector, but that's all I know about it. I saw that the persons involved were those who were otherwise engaged in the investigations into war crimes, and that's how I can conclude that it was they in fact who were in charge of these centres and conducted their basic investigations there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you conclude for the possibility that the collection centre in Knin and the reception centre in Knin were located on the same premises? Which would mean, if it is a school that both were in that school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can merely say that, with regard to the collection centre for civilians, I'm sure that it was clearly separate from the collection centre. But whether or not it was in the same building, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us that it was clearly separate, you must have some idea, isn't it, about their locations? Otherwise, it's difficult to say that they were clearly separate. A direct question: Were they in the same premises, a school? Were they or were they not, to the extent you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still cannot remember that because I know that the civil protection was engaged in the support of the population that was taken to the reception centres for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I seek from our interpreters, because the Chamber has looked at the original documents now and then. A while ago the witness talked about a collection centre for civilians. Could we hear from our interpreters what word was translated in this context, that is collection centre for civilians. Was that sabirni centre? Could I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters understood the witness to have said sabirni centre, that is collection centre for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... then added for civilians, which means that that this term apparently in some context is -- well, let me not comment on it at this at this moment. I just wanted to know whether there would be any possibility of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could check that, Mr. President. I don't think, if you read the sentence in its entirety, it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, I asked specifically, our interpreters. And if you want to verify that, you know that there is audio available in the original to verify what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I would simply -- if you wish, I will do it in redirect. But this sentence doesn't make sense as it currently stands, in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, have you a possibility to ask any further questions. Mr. Carrier, I leave it further in your hands at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not -- I have not exhausted this subject, but I just wanted to see whether some questions could put to the witness and that we could receive some answers, hopefully without being engaged in too many procedural issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, the purpose of citing his evidence so far is that the foundation has been laid from the information from before. And the Prosecution is clearly under an obligation under Rule 90(H) to put contrary evidence to him. I don't plan to educate him but taking him through pieces of evidence, but simply to put at least contrary information to him. So that was the purpose of the style of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say you would have to put your case to the witness if you are eliciting from him evidence which contradicts your case in which is not in direct response what has been dealt with in chief, Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going cite Rule 90(H) myself, Mr. President. The witness, if there is an evidentiary foundation for the Prosecution's position, then that evidentiary basis should be put to the witness to give him an opportunity to refute it. But to simply make a general assertion and then ask the witness whether he agrees with the general assertion doesn't, in our view, provide much probative value as to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, do you understand and/or speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, as I announced earlier, there was a document, a report on a conversation you have had which is available in your language. The Chamber thought that this might be an appropriate time to invite to you read that but not in this courtroom. Would you be willing to go through the document, and if there's anything inaccurate in it, it's not a verbatim report on what you said, but whether if you would say that the gist of what you are reported to have said is incorrect, that you inform us about it. Would you, for those purposes, please follow Madam Usher and read that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to resolve what should and should not be put to this witness. We can't recount all of the evidence but, of course, there are portions of evidence. I remember the evidence of a lady who said that she was taken to -- I think she said, but forgive me I'm wrong, to the school in Knin where she had to wait for 40 days. She was not allowed to leave, at least that's my recollection. I have not checked that. And then was taken to Zadar, I think it was a lady together with her daughter. So that is evidence which at least suggests strongly that she was taken there against her will. We -- I think we also have documentary evidence, in which the word detention or detainees is used. And I'll not go through all of it at this moment, but there certainly are pieces of evidence which would contradict what this witness said, and -- because he said that never anyone was taken against his will to such a centre, apart from how the centre should be qualified, what name they should bear, where they were located, close to each other, not close to each other. This witness is talking about 900 persons processed apparently through the reception centre or collection centre for civilians in Knin. Is there any way that we could agree on what is fair to put to the witness and what is not fair to put to the witness against the background of what I just said and which is certainly not an exhaustive -- is not an exhaustive reflection of all of the evidence which is directly or indirectly related to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, from my perspective the issues are much simpler than perhaps they may appear at first glance. In my direct, I literally lifted verbatim from the Prosecution's pre-trial brief on reception centres. And I posed four questions that are the Prosecution's case from its pre-trial brief. I asked him, Were the reception centres set up as part of a plan to remove Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Were Serb civilians forced to stay in these centres? Was fear deliberately instilled in the Serbs civilians in the centres? And were they systematically transferred out of Croatia after being in the centres? I raised a fifth point which was that there no international criticism in the reception centres in 1995. If the Prosecution wishes to impeach him on those claims, then I there is a proper process to impeach him on that case whether they wish to use statements of witnesses who have appeared, whether there is documentary evidence, et cetera. It is it improper, though, for council to get up and say, The record says this, and how do you address that? If they want to say there was a plan, that needs to be put to this witness. The issue of whether -- and Mrs. A said she felt that she was held against her will might be relevant to one of these points but doesn't address the overall picture, which is this is a JCE allegation. He is the person at the top responsible for establishing and running the centres. And in the overall scheme of a joint criminal enterprise, I think the Prosecution needs to put their case as to -- as it concerns a JCE to the witness. How they wish to go about it is up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of that case is that people were detained against their will, whether this finally amounts to a plan, of course, is also the case, but you don't have to put the whole case to the witness. What you should put to the witness that he testified about never a person being taken there. He said there was no plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness, and I could be easily wrong here, I believe he said he didn't know of a person being forced against their will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- which is different from saying that a no one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, however, the Prosecution's case that one or more persons were taken there against their will. So then it is fair that that would be put to the witness. And I think would also be fair to put the witness the documentary evidence which specifically focuses on who should stay in what kind of centre and whether it is it about detention of civilians. You'll understand, Mr. Carrier, I don't have all the sources ready because I prepare in a different way for these court hearings than the parties do. Also this Chamber, of course, has no case to be put to the witness because this Chamber has no case. Therefore, we ask questions in a bit of a different way. I think it would be fair to raise the issue about -- that we have received evidence of a lady who reports that she was detained, and if you have any other examples, you can summarize it, and we can't go through all of the evidence. Further, I remember, and have you to forgive me not having all the P numbers present, but I have a clear recollection of a document in which centres and civilians being there and whether to be kept there or not to be kept there, appears. I think it would be fair at least to put those two matters to the witness and to say the witness that it's the Prosecution's case that people were not voluntarily staying in those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I have to admit, Mr. President, I'm slightly confused on a couple of points. And if I could just seek clarification and explain why. The first being under Rule 90(H) the reason -- in the cross-examination of a witness who is able -- I'm sure you know this, and I apologise for -- partly it is for my own benefit. But in the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the -- for the cross-examining party, council shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears. So my understanding of that was, number one, that it was simply to put the nature, not specific pieces of evidence. And I appreciate your point, Your Honour, but then in background to this in preparation, my understanding is that Defence have also objected to saying, well, putting it to a witness, well, this person said X or that person said this. And it was also objected today that when I read things saying, well, it's in evidence, so that was objected to, I should just say -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So that's why I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware of that. Could we try to find a fair mixture that putting it in a general terms to the witness that this -- the case of the Prosecution is that people were not -- at least not all of them were staying there. We heard evidence of someone who was taken to a Knin centre, in a school building, from what I remember, and that apparently contradicts your testimony, do you have any comment on that? And perhaps the documentary evidence could be specifically put to him. I -- there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. If -- and just for the record, if the Prosecution contends that there was international criticism of the reception centres, if that could be put to him, because he is the person in charge of them, and then can he deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would, in addition, put that to the witness as well, whether there was any international --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Misetic already did that; he said no. So you're saying if there's evidence -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... He said no, but isn't it true that in cross-examination you try to challenge the credibility and reliability of a witness. So if it is the position of the Prosecution if a witness has testified about a matter in chief, that there's no need to further explore whether he -- his answers were in accordance with the truth, then it would come as a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That wasn't my position. It was simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's what you said, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think my point is that the reason that I've tried to construct it in a certain way is to try to address the things that he's mentioned, which is why I read it him first, as I explained, to try to hit those points but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we take a break at this moment, that you try within the next 20 minutes to reach, and I have tried to broker a bit, to achieve an agreement with Mr. Misetic on what is appropriately put to the witness and what is not necessary to put to the witness, and then ask him questions. And then I'd also like to know how much time you would further need.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: This was the -- the last bit. It's taken longer than expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question would be to Mr. Misetic and other Defence counsel, whether what happened during cross-examination has changed their estimate as to how much would be needed in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think it is exactly what you said yesterday, Mr. President. Maybe up to ten minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. If this Chamber comes back after the break, we expect a smooth conclusion of the cross-examination. The parties are invited to assist each other in making this happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think on behalf of all of the parties we would like to see you come back after the break, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you would like to contradict what Mr. Misetic just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all, Your Honour. I would just like to add that based on cross-examination from my learned colleague, I'll need probably ten minutes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Let's then try to do the following. We resume at five minutes to 6.00. Mr. Carrier will certainly conclude within, then, the next ten to 15 minutes. Then it is quarter past 6.00. Mr. Misetic would take another ten minutes. Mr. Mikulicic would take another ten minutes, which brings us to 6.35. I include already that you take a bit more, and the Chamber would at least have 15 to 20 minutes to deal with some procedural matters at the end of this afternoon's hearing. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, regarding the reception centres, did you ever visit any of these reception centres on ground in the first few weeks of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did you visit any of them during August, at all, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, you have provided evidence that people were allowed to leave these reception centres that you were in charge of, of their own free will. This Chamber has heard evidence, for example, Exhibit P30, paragraph 2, P1099, paragraphs 20 to 21 - and, sorry, page 2 on P30 - at a reception centre in Knin there was about 150 women, children, elderly, and that the Deputy Commander of that place in Knin told people from the UN that these 150 people were not free to leave, and that was for their own security. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our instructions how civilians in reception centres should be treated were contrary to such a statement. I know that civilians were able to leave the centre when they wanted to and some did, indeed, leave and return to their homes. In the first few days, on the 6th or 7th August, around that time, I issued an explicit instruction for civilians in reception centre -- centres to be allowed to leave such a centre, if -- if relatives come to pick them up. And in that -- in that context, I demanded that, once communication is set up between these civilians and their family, the Red Cross be involved, which has a tracing service. The Red Cross, being a humanitarian organisation, upon request of the civilians in the centres, searched for their relatives who were willing to accept them. So that was a way to leave for such civilians, they could go and stay with their relatives. We considered that the most secure possibility at that time. Anyway, civilians were completely free to decide whether they wanted to stay in the centre or join their relatives or return their villages; that is, the places where they lived before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now your answer says that you issued an order that people be allowed to leave the centre if relatives come and pick them up, in that context. And then you talk about --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... getting the Red Cross involved.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that you're actually setting conditions for whether or not they can leave so they're not actually free to leave, under your order?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is natural that such people were asked the question whether they have anybody in the Republic of Croatia to who they wanted to go. And there were requests by people to join their relatives. And it was possible to forward such a request through the Red Cross to their relatives, and upon the receipt of the reply, stating that the relatives were willing to accept them, we let these people go, and people did leave. I spoke to Mr. Cemerin and learned that in the early days, some from our centre went -- well, let's call it a camp of the UN at Knin. People from that camp came to our camp, and that is the essence of my statement, that they were able to leave the reception centre of the civil protection if they so wished. People who wanted to return to their homes as soon as possible, to them, we clearly -- we made it clear that in those areas there might be some -- some threats to their security, but we were in no position to prevent them from returning home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, this Chamber has received evidence that people on arrival in Knin were told by police to go to a school building in Knin and, at that place, they were held, and during that time they were guarded by policemen wearing uniforms with guns, and that they were not allowed to leave. And that's after they had been actually stopped and held in a basement first before being moved to Knin. And the reference for that is P652, paragraph 17; P653, paragraph 11; P654. Transcript reference 6718 and following. And though I cite some of the evidence, I'm being selective because clearly, and just for the record, I can't be comprehensive in terms of this so ... but I'm putting pieces of it to you. So do you have any comment on that? And actually before do you that, let me just -- there's also evidence that people gather in the Knin elementary school, older people, sick people, and there's a commentary by an international that it was strange that there were 150 heavily armed and very aggressive police people for 130 old people. And that is D741, page 11. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment to that. I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And some people -- there's also evidence that this Trial Chamber has heard about people who were actually forced to leave their houses in the countryside, and they were put in collection centres by the military. That's P31, page 1, paragraph 2. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has also received evidence from different Croatian authorities on the ground about collecting civilians and handing them over to the Ministry of Interior, and there's a number of different reasons, and I will go through them with you. D57, one person noted that people were collected in order to give them identification and also because there were some security concerns. That's also at P897. A soldier reported that the default measure for civilians found in the area was to transfer them to collection centres for security reasons and to register them and conduct investigations, et cetera, to see if they had any connection to enemy forces. There's evidence from military police that testified they picked up people. Sometimes it was because -- to protect them from harm; sometimes it was so they could get ID. And that's at transcript reference 9128 and following. More police evidence that military or police brought civilians because they were incapable of living on their own. Some had been abandoned, some were brought there voluntarily, some for their own safety. That was all actually from one person. P897, paragraph 35; and also transcript reference T9292. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning civilians who were in reception centres, we interviewed them and collected information to issue them civilian documents. It was required for that to get a document about the Croatian citizenship, et cetera, so the procedure to establish their -- their civil position was conducted. When it comes to persons who were incapable of living alone and had no one to take care of them, and I suppose those were mostly persons who were unable to move, they were taken to the centres in vehicles. Whether that was done by the police or civil protection, I don't know. That may have differed from case to case. I know of some instances where such people were transported by the civil protection, and there is no reason to suppose that in some instances the police may have done so, on the occasion of patrolling the ground. When it comes to the activities of the military police, I cannot comment that. Generally speaking, I can say that the reason stated for protecting their security was something that everybody had warned of and with good reason, because it was a very large area and with scattered villages or hamlets that sometimes were made up of only a few -- of only a few houses, and some of them lived alone or in households with two or three persons. But it is clear that offers to stay safely at such a reception centre was something that was reasonable to suggest to such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Who decided which people were in incapable of taking care of themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such decisions weren't taken, but if you found someone abandoned lying on their bed in a house or wherever, unable to move, you would certainly suggest to that person or plead, for sanitary reasons or even for providing food regularly, to transport that person to a centre where medical and other care would be provided to them. Food would be provided and hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And in relation to what you just said, is it the case that simply the need to provide food for people on a regular basis was sufficient to bring them to the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the decisive factor. But at any rate, I know of no single instance when the civil protection, that is our people in the field, that they brought anybody to the reception centre forcibly. We spoke to the people and explained them -- the situation to them. They were simply left alone at the places where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And this issuing an ID and interviews, et cetera, about establishing people's, I suppose, nationality, did that happen at reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In police stations, there were administrative services, which, in our terminology, means regulating the civil status of persons. That is, citizenship, issuing personal identification documents, or driving licences, passports, and any other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for a second. I just want to know, did it happen in reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is impossible to issue such documents in reception centres. We interviewed the people there, and the people produced the documents they had. And based on those documents, checks were conducted in police -- in the police administrations, in order to establish whether the person in question was born in Croatia, whether he or she had lived in Croatia all the time, and everything else that had to be established to grant citizenship to someone. Once the documents were made, if those persons were in the reception centres, they were handed to those persons, and whoever was able to move, went to the police station to receive their documents because receiving such a document requires signing a form, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, this Chamber has received evidence that from ECMM reports - this is P815, paragraph 2 - that Croat authorities are taking the Serbs to so-called collection centres in Gospic and Zadar for the purpose of registration. And then it said: "But this procedure has not yet caught all the people." And the Chamber has also received evidence - this is from Flynn - that he -- he was trying to get access to people that were kept in -- in a school in Knin, that he had taken this up with General Cermak. That's at T1241. Do you have any comment or any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned collection centres. I have already said that during that period, such centres were not under the jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My question was, he was trying to get access to people who were kept in a school in Knin, and I wondered if you had any comment on that. I am sorry, I do apologise. I was looking at the wrong thing. I did say collection centres. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if international monitors, observers, were faced with any obstacles to enter collection centres for civilians. But having read the documents that you gave me and that refer to a meeting with UN officials, I can say that at the UN centre in Knin, two or three days after the end of combat actions, international observers suggested to the population that happened to be there, to go to civil protection centre to regulate their status. That is, their civil status. Whether or not the observers had to produce a document that civil protection required them to show at the entrance to the centre, I don't know. Many people were roaming the place, wearing various uniforms. It is probable that civil protection wanted to check who wants to enter such a centre or leave it, or intends to stay there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not on the record, but I was looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I'm just trying to sift through the evidence. There is quite a few -- obviously there is quite a few pieces of evidence, so I was trying to pick ones that were representative or fair enough, given that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I consult ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I think before the break I asked for a kind of a mix. I think it would be fair at this moment to put to the witness that his testimony about the reception centres where civilians stayed at the time is quite different from the evidence, at least quite different from some of the evidence that was produced by the Prosecution, which, as may have been clear from the witness from now -- up till now, that these reception centres were not places where people went voluntarily, but that they were kept there for a shorter and longer period of time and that they were not free to go, as the witness testified, and then ask a general comment because we could go into details for ages now. Because we have, of course, heard quite some answers from the witness, which go all in a direction quite different from what the Prosecution thinks these centres were. So, therefore, if you conclude in a more general way, because, otherwise, we -- I don't know whether this in any way violates the agreement between the parties, but there comes a point where --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think you have the right to violation our agreement, so I have no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no problem with it. Mr. Cayley, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't want to cut into time here, but I do have to state that, for example, the use of evidence in confronting the witness on page 65, line 18, where the statement was made, There's also evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard about people who were actually forced to leave their homes, houses, in the country side, and they were put in collection centres by the military. And the reference for that is P31. Well, when one looks at, P31 which is an HRAT report from August 10th, there is a statement saying, Persons at the school in Knin have started to leave, about 130 of 250 so far with safe passage cards, "propusnicas," issued by the Ministry of Defence. And then there's a discussion below that says: "One woman reported being forced to leave her house in the countryside." I mean, that's the kind of thing that's problematic about this, Your Honour, and you know that -- I raise that simply to draw the Court's attention to that one instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for doing that. It may well be that Mr. Carrier has not -- at all instances he referred to, has achieved the accuracy one would wish to achieve in this respect. I think, however, that the -- what was put to the witness in more general terms, and the answers of the witness sufficiently assist the Chamber so as not to urge Mr. Carrier to proceed in this way. Mr. Carrier, I earlier asked you to come to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just respond to that, because I'm just looking at it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I asked you to conclude, and otherwise we will be here still at 7.30. I do understand that you might not be fully happy with it. If there is any need to further explore this matter, you make written submissions on the matter. It is not at this moment assisting us in receiving the evidence from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour, just following on from what my learned friend Mr. Kuzmanovic said. It's the reference that Mr. Carrier gave in respect of my client. And if the Chamber -- I'm not going to read it out, because I don't want to waste anybody's time, but if you look at the reference on page 1241, and it's not exactly what Mr. Carrier is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are -- the questions have been put; the questions have been answered. And there is some criticism, which will not at this moment, I take it, change the testimony of this witness. And if you want to respond to that later, Mr. Carrier, you will have an opportunity to do so in all fairness. But let's try to proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, had you a chance to look at that UN document during the break; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And what you read there, is that an accurate record of your meeting between the UN on the 23rd of November, 1995? Do you have any comments on that or ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only two minor points to make. At item 4, it says the authorities provided their assistance to prevent them from leaving, and a special agreement was signed with the HVO. Well, I don't know if that is exactly what I said and whether this is this exactly how I put it, and whether the two points were part of the same context, so I would place a reservation on the sentence, although I don't consider it decisive. At item 8, paragraph 2, it says: "Mr. Zidovec pointed out that in the course of Operation Storm more than 105 civilian policemen and explosive experts did their job in a dedicated and professional way. Of course, the number must be a typo. Or perhaps Mr. Mamadi Diakite misheard the figure. As for the rest, I think that it accurately reflects the topics discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to sum it up, the evidence that this Chamber has so far received -- is quite different from your evidence on what reception centres were there for and whether or not people could leave, et cetera. They weren't free to go, as you said. They were kept there, on our evidence, by armed people, and they were brought there against their will. And I just wondered whether you had any final comment on the evidence in terms of that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is that it is only natural that such statements, I mean, the statements made by me and the documents you have, differ. Now, whether this will serve to complete the picture or whether you will have at your disposal or whether you will be hearing statements that will disprove the statements that were made to you and that differ from mine, that's something that I cannot pass a judgement on. What I would like to say at this point is that by the end of 1995, by which time I performed the duties of civilian protection, I had never, from a single international organisation, including EU monitors, ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and other humanitarian organisations present and active in the area for various reasons, heard any comments which would call into question the legality of actions taken by members of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Carrier. Mr. Misetic, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could have -- well, let me ask first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, are you, or did you receive information about how many people were entering and exiting the reception centres in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure is roughly 4.100 civilians who went through, passed through reception centres. According to the final data of the civilian protection, as part of Operation Povratak, for the year 1995, the centre in Knin accounted for roughly 1.000 of these 4.000 individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you -- as you sit here today, would you know how many persons had passed through the Zadar reception centre as of September 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information exists, but I cannot, unfortunately, remember it. Compared to the numbers for other reception centres, I think that the number is fairly lower than for the Knin centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P2357, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, I don't want to interrupt. But I'm just trying to figure out how this is a re-direct, was this something that was raised during the cross-examination that couldn't have been put to him in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think you'll see it directly relates to the issues of whether people were free to leave, which is a topic Mr. Carrier covered now within the last hour. And what those numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, these are the statistics for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was the matter raised in cross for the first time, or was it -- I mean, was it a matter which came up during cross-examination and was not in any way touched upon in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it has to be -- to re-direct that it had been touch on in chief. The issue was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you deal with the matter in chief then, of course, you can -- I think in re-direct any matter that arose during cross-examination, but not everything to go over the same ground again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only have ten means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, if you look on this document, this is it now the statistics for the -- the reception centres and where people were or where they went to after passing through them. If you look at the column for Zadar, it gives you the statistics. 366 were still in the centres, seven placed in hospital, blank sent back to flats. And in the original you'll see blank left to Serbia. 543 left to relatives or friends. And then there's a total on the bottom. Is that consistent, Mr. Zidovec, with what your understanding was of where people were going and whether they could leave once they entered the reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course, they could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was -- was there -- do you recall any issue regarding the use of terminology, collection centre versus reception centre, and that that issue had to be addressed by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, since I had the opportunity to have a look at the document of my meeting with UN representatives, I remembered that, at the time, for the term used here as collection centre, we in fact used the term detention centre; whereas, reception centre was the venue receiving civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to pull up a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, it's Exhibit P914.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And just ask you if you recall having seen this document or have any knowledge about it. It's a document from the crime police sector, 8 August 1995, and if you look towards the bottom: "We are hereby informing you that in the future, instead of the term collection centre for prisoners of war, you are to use the term admissions centre for prisoners of war" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic asked the question if he know anything about reception versus collection centres and if there was ever a need by the Ministry of Interior to deal with that. He said no. He is now showing him a document, now he's reading him the document, without actually asking if he had seen it first. And he's basically telling him what it says, which is leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could have asked the question. You may know that I'm concerned, and not only me, with the terminology used here. Do under those circumstances, it might have been one of our questions, so we'll let Mr. Misetic go for a time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, my question to you is, you see that the last sentence, it says: "Instead of the term 'admission centre,' you are to use the term 'reception centre for civilians.'" Since the reception centres were part of your portfolio, does this refresh your recollection as to whether there was issue of the terminology used within the MUP for how your reception centres were supposed to be designated? If you don't recall, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that the reception centre for civilians was never in dispute, as a term. It was never controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did the International Committee of the Red Cross have access to the reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite understandable. They would come either individually or with representatives of the Croatian Red Cross. By virtue of its status, the ICRC is entitled to interact with all civilians in reception centres. There was nothing disputable about that, and it was quite clear to all involved that they have unimpeded access.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings or receive with or receive any reports from the ICRC in August or September 1995, as it relates to collection centres -- I'm sorry, reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to attend meetings with a delegation of the ICRC in the course of these months in Zagreb, because back in 1995, I was one of the vice-presidents of the Croatian Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in that -- those meetings with the delegation of the ICRC, did it -- was it brought to your attention that there was some dispute by the ICRC about how -- about the conditions of the reception centres, and whether people were -- had -- people's liberties were being restricted within them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said and I confirm now that we had never received any objections to the treatment of civilians in reception centres from any of the international organisation, including the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, due to the circumstances, I give up. I will pose no questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check, have the two documents you thought should be put to the witness, they have been put to the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They have not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, in order to avoid -- you know that there were two out of the five which caused Mr. Misetic some problems. The other three, no objection against admission, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same, too, for the other Defence teams. Mr. Carrier, two out of the five meet objections. You can do two things. Either await for the decision of the Chamber, once we have reviewed the documents; or stay on the safe side, put them to the witness where apparently then, Mr. Misetic, no objections will further exist; or withdraw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the assistance of counsel, it is P2576 and P2577, which are 65 ter 7338 and 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just trying to look through it. I'll just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any questions on P2577, which was 65 ter 7339.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, do you insist on putting it to the witness in order give up your objections against admission, or is it sufficiently dealt with by the terminology questions you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll waive my objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll waive your objections in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both, yes. That's fine. Mr. Carrier, I think you showed a UN document to the witness, he received a copy in his own language. That has not been tendered, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if it was MFI'd or not, but if it hasn't, then could we please tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't MFI'd, but it would become Exhibit P2580, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against admission? There are no objections. Therefore, P2580 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please state the numbers of the five MFI documents which were tendered as bar table documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's P2575 up to and including P2579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one final -- perhaps two final questions for you, Mr. Zidovec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us, you gave us the picture of old people on their bed not being able to move, starving, not able to look after themselves. Is that anything concrete that was reported to you, or is that what you thought might have been the case when people were taken to reception centres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My attention was particularly drawn to several such cases by members of the civilian protection, because they wanted centres for social welfare and other local government bodies to take care of these individuals, since it was impossible for the civilian protection to provide for these peoples in the long-term. This involved medical care, the -- maintaining hygiene standards, and a number of other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this done orally, or is there any document which provides such a report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One document which the chief of the civilian protection department, Mr. Cemerin, sent to me, and which constituted an overview of the situation as he saw it roughly on the 11th of August, referred to a great many problems encountered by civilian protection officers in such cases, as well as the problems they encountered in trying to transfer such individuals to the care of social welfare centres and other similar institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware of people taken from reception centres to such institutions to further take care of their social welfare? Specific instances.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZIDOVEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I am not aware of it. As soon as the individuals came under the care of such institutions, they fell within the purview of the Ministry of Health and their structures within the local government and administration. They were no longer within the care of the Ministry of the Interior, the social protection -- the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you -- thank you for that answer. Mr. Zidovec, this concludes your testimony in this court. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would not be wise at this moment to deal with procedural matters. Although we have find time for it, perhaps tomorrow, if we try to do with continue the first 15 minutes in the afternoon, which would mean that we would start late, and I'm certain that we would not need more than 15 minutes for it. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Thursday, the 9th of July, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
